# Guess the Number with Duke

Duke, the Java mascot, is thinking of a whole number from 1 to 10. You get five
guesses. Guess right and Duke jumps for joy.

The backend is Jakarta EE 11 on Open Liberty. The front end is plain HTML, CSS,
and JavaScript.

Built from [BRD.md](BRD.md), [jakarta-ee-prompt.txt](jakarta-ee-prompt.txt), and
[demo-prompt-common.md](demo-prompt-common.md), the copies of the requirements
and the generation prompt this project was built against.

## Requirements

JDK 25 and Maven 3.9 or newer. Open Liberty and every Jakarta EE API come down
from Maven on the first build, so nothing has to be installed first.

## Running it

Every command here runs from this directory, not from the repository root. The
root holds one directory per demo and no POM of its own, so Maven has nothing to
build there.

```bash
cd jakarta-ee-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn liberty:dev
```

That starts Liberty in dev mode and serves the game at <http://localhost:9080>.
Dev mode watches the sources, so edits to Java, the front end, or `server.xml`
land without a restart. Press `Ctrl-C` to stop.

To build the WAR and run the whole suite, unit tests and integration tests both:

```bash
cd jakarta-ee-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn verify
```

That packages `target/jakarta-ee-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1.war`, starts Liberty,
plays real games against it, and shuts it down again.

If something else on the machine already holds port 9080, Liberty will start but
never bind, and the integration tests will report that the server answered with
something other than JSON. Move the ports instead:

```bash
cd jakarta-ee-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn liberty:dev -Dliberty.var.http.port=9081 -Dliberty.var.https.port=9444
mvn verify -Dliberty.var.http.port=9081 -Dliberty.var.https.port=9444
```

## Running the tests

```bash
cd jakarta-ee-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn test -DskipITs
```

The unit tests cover the rules, the session, the wording, and the JSON shape,
and they run in about two seconds because none of them needs a container. `mvn
verify` adds the integration tests, which play over real HTTP against a running
Liberty.

The server draws its own secret number, so the integration tests cannot be told
what it is. The win test halves the range from the high and low feedback, which
can only ever win if that feedback is right. The lose test needs a game whose
opening guess misses, so it deals again on the one game in ten that is won on
the opening guess, giving up after twenty deals.

## How it fits together

```
src/main/java/tech/virtua/duke/
  game/                The rules, as plain Java with no container in sight
    GameRules            The three fixed numbers: 1, 10, and five guesses
    GuessingGame         One round, from the opening draw to the win or the loss
    GameSnapshot         A game as the player is allowed to see it
    GameStatus           ACTIVE, WON, LOST
    GuessFeedback        NONE, TOO_LOW, TOO_HIGH, CORRECT
    SubmissionOutcome    What the game did with a submission
    Submission           An outcome and the game it left behind
    GuessParser          Whatever the player typed, read as a guess or as nothing
    SecretNumberPicker   Where the secret number comes from
  web/                 The HTTP surface
    GameResource         The three endpoints
    PlayerGame           The one game belonging to a browser session
    GameView             The JSON shape every answer takes
    GameMessages         The sentence the player reads
    GuessRequest         The submitted guess
    UnreadableGuessMapper   Turns a body the server cannot read into that same answer
    SecretNumberSource   Produces the picker, keeping CDI out of the game package

src/main/webapp/                     index.html, css, js, and Duke
src/main/liberty/config/server.xml   Liberty features and ports
```

The rules live in `GuessingGame`, which knows nothing about HTTP, CDI, or JSON.
That is what lets most of the suite run in milliseconds. A `GuessingGame` never
changes: every submission answers with the game that follows it, and
`PlayerGame` swaps the whole game in one compare-and-set, so two requests racing
each other on one session cannot leave a guess half applied.

`PlayerGame` is `@SessionScoped`, which is the whole of the session handling —
no cookie to mint, no map of games to sweep. Liberty's `httpSession`
configuration marks the cookie `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax`.

The server owns every rule, including what counts as a legal guess. The guess is
submitted as text rather than as a number precisely so the server gets to
decide: the page sends whatever was typed and renders whatever comes back.

## The API

Every endpoint answers with the same JSON, so the page renders any answer the
same way.

| Request | Answers | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/game` | `200` | The game in play, dealing one if this browser is new |
| `POST /api/game/new` | `200` | Abandons the game in play and deals a fresh one |
| `POST /api/game/guess` | `200` | The guess counted |
| | `400` | Not a whole number from 1 to 10, so it did not count |
| | `409` | The game was already over |

A guess looks like this:

```bash
curl -i -c jar -b jar -X POST http://localhost:9080/api/game/guess \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"guess": "7"}'
```

The `-c`/`-b` cookie jar matters. The game lives in the HTTP session, so a client
that drops cookies is dealt a brand new game on every call.

An answer:

```json
{
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "outcome": "COUNTED",
  "feedback": "TOO_LOW",
  "message": "3 is too low. Try something higher — 4 guesses left.",
  "guessesMade": 1,
  "guessesRemaining": 4,
  "guessLimit": 5,
  "lowestNumber": 1,
  "highestNumber": 10,
  "lastGuess": 3,
  "secretNumber": null
}
```

`status` is `ACTIVE`, `WON`, or `LOST`. `outcome` says what the request itself
did: `COUNTED`, `NOT_A_VALID_NUMBER`, `GAME_ALREADY_OVER`, or `NONE` for a
request that only read the game. `secretNumber` stays `null` until the game is
over.

## The front end

`index.html`, `css/styles.css`, and `js/app.js` are served straight out of the
WAR. Guesses can be entered and submitted with the keyboard alone, the form is
deliberately `novalidate` so the server's friendly wording does the talking
instead of a browser tooltip, and the message is a live region so screen readers
announce it. Every text and control color clears the 4.5:1 contrast benchmark in
both the light and dark palettes.

Answers can arrive out of order, so each request takes a ticket and only the
newest one is allowed to draw. Without that, a slow guess could land after a new
game and put the finished one back on screen. A guess already on its way is left
to finish on its own: a second one is ignored until it lands, so two quick presses
of Enter cannot spend two guesses while the page shows only one of them.

Duke is the official artwork from the
[OpenJDK Duke project](https://github.com/openjdk/duke): `Thinking` while he
holds the number, `Wave` when he celebrates. The only change to the artwork is a
cropped `viewBox`, so he scales without the original page margins. The win
animation is three shrinking hops with a tilt over 1.5 seconds, ending back in
the resting pose. It runs once, never blocks the New game button, and is turned
off under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
